en: The Fourth Fascicle of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-alaṃkāra-bhāṣya*:

An Exposition on the Meaning of Severing the Bonds (*saṃyojana*), Analyzed in Seven Sections. 1. Explanation of Names. 2. Essential Nature (*svabhāva*). 3. Distinctions in the Treatment and Severance. 4. Similarities and Differences in Contemplative Practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). 5. Analysis of Regression and Non-regression. 6. The Number and Quantity of Categories. 7.
The Stages and Levels of Treatment and Severance.
First, regarding the explanation of the name:
"severing the fetters" (prahāṇa-saṃyojana). "Fetters" (saṃyojana) refers to that which binds and constrains.
The various obstacles of affliction and ignorance bind the practitioner within and without the realms, preventing liberation; therefore, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"If a person practices the cultivation of detachment from the desire realm, yet their body remains bound within the form realm."
Even up to the point of practicing to emerge from the formless realm, one sees the body bound within the *ālaya*.
This is the meaning of "bondage," which is synonymous with "knot.
"Severing" refers to the act of cutting off and eliminating it.
It is said that the sages "sever" because they sever all fetters and bonds by means of the path of the three vehicles;
thus, "fetters and hindrances" (saṃyojana-nīvaraṇa) are designated as "severing" (prahāṇa) based on their realization.
Here, "severing" refers to that which is realized.
The fetters are precisely that which is to be abandoned.
As for the second nature, it is the essential substance of the dharma that abandons the fetters.
The *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* states:
"The application of relinquishment has two parts:
first, the part of obstacles."
Second is the section on remediation.
When an obstruction has matured, it must be discarded,
just as a boil that has ripened must be lanced.
When it is processed, it must be used;
just as when food is cooked, it must be eaten.
The treatise further states:
The transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) involves both relinquishment and attainment.
Relinquishment refers to being free from the two obstacles;
attainment refers to acquiring the two types of wisdom.
Now, to explain this in full, there are three meanings.
The first is that which is capable of severing:
namely, the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of the noble paths of the Three Vehicles.
Second, that which is to be abandoned:
the various afflictions of the two obstacles, namely those of ignorance and those of defilement.
Third, that which is to be realized.
This refers to suchness (*tathatā*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Within this, all three meanings encompass the Four Noble Truths;
first, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The second is the truth of the origin of suffering;
the third is the truth of cessation.
Regarding the third [topic], the distinctions in the methods of treatment and abandonment, there is an analysis by way of four gates.
First, analysis according to consciousness;
second, analysis according to the time periods;
third, analysis by way of the paths.
Fourth, the subduing and severance of conceptual discrimination.
Regarding the first point, concerning consciousness, there are three meanings.

First, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, both ordinary beings and sages sever delusions by employing wisdom that arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to cut off all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This [wisdom] comprises both mundane and outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*),
and does not employ the five sensory consciousnesses.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
At the time of detachment from desire and at the time of falling away;
likewise at birth and at death; as well as at the moment of severance and the moment of reconnection.
One should know that this refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Vibhāṣā* also state this.
Since the treatises already state that the abandonment of desire pertains exclusively to the mental consciousness.
It should be known that the severing of the fetters is accomplished by the wisdom co-arising with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
and not by those five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), because those five consciousnesses consist of only a single moment.
Because they take specific characteristics as their object,
and because they rely on the establishment of reality,
ordinary persons do not sever afflictions within the conventional world.
The sages sever afflictions only through noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*).
This wisdom capable of severing [afflictions] does not coexist with the six consciousnesses,
because according to that school, those consciousnesses are associated with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Based on the fourth [level], one relies on the wisdom of the final moment of the practice-mind for right abandonment.
Regarding the three [levels], they rely on the Mahāyāna,
which extensively explains the nine consciousnesses.
If one speaks of correct governance (*samyak-pratipatti*), it is likewise only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The Bodhisattva, regarding wholesome consciousness, remains detached from the other five consciousnesses."
The commentary on the lower section states:

"A virtuous consciousness" refers to the untainted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Distant from the five [sensory] consciousnesses" means being free from the five types of distraction as well as being free from the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
It is asked:
Therefore, the severance of delusions is not accomplished by other consciousnesses.
The answer is:
the essence of the first pure consciousness is suchness (tathatā).
The true nature is inherently present and is not a wisdom produced by initial cultivation;
it does not involve the severing of afflictions.
The ālayavijñāna contains only the seeds of pure qualities resulting from hearing the熏 (xūn, perfuming).
Because of this, one cannot manifest the practice of illuminating the principles to sever the fetters.
A question is asked:
If the hearing-perfuming within the fundamental consciousness is not the correct severance, [how can it lead to liberation?]
Why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that "inferior-grade hearing-perfuming can counteract superior-grade fundamental consciousness, and so on,
up to superior-grade hearing-perfuming which can counteract inferior-grade fundamental consciousness"?
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
"The permeation of hearing arises for the purpose of diminishing the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), not for the purpose of augmenting it."
Regarding the force of that treatise, which states that "the hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) can act as an antidote," how is it that this is not [itself] a correct abandonment?
The answer is:

the statement that the hearing-perfuming acts as an antidote to the three grades of afflictions and to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is based on the fact that the hearing-perfuming can generate the counteractive factors (*pratipakṣa*).
This is called an "antidote" in the sense of being a counteragent,
but it is not the actual antidote itself.
The ādāna-vijñāna is constantly born together with the four afflictions as its defilements.
However, that which is abandoned is not the antidote.
Because the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are distracted, indeterminate, and arise for only a single moment, they are not the antidote.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The five consciousnesses are not the locus where the path of counteraction arises.
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* further states:

"Wholesome consciousness refers to the untainted mental consciousness, distinct from the five consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness. Second, [this is] distinguished according to the [three] time periods.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the path of counteraction and the delusions that are to be abandoned do not coexist.
When correct understanding is present,
the delusions exist in the past or the future.

Now, by means of the antidote directed toward the present, one correctly treats the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions of the present; thus, the entity of the affliction—which is a factor that is neither form nor mind—is caused to lose its status as an acquired object and fails to be established.
It is called "severing delusion" (prahāṇa),
but this does not mean that it directly severs the substantial entity of defiled delusion.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
If one does not abandon [the defilements], it cannot be called an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Second, according to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
when the path of the antidote arises, it correctly abandons the functional capacity (*śakti*) of past and future afflictions.
The reason for this is precisely that wisdom,
by severing the capacity of past afflictions to act as causes, prevents the principle of their future fruits from arising;
thus, it is said that when the cause perishes, the fruit is extinguished, which is termed "severing the fetters."
Yet there is no dharma-substance of the fetters (saṃyojana) and proclivities (anuśaya) that can be severed.
Third, according to the Mahāyāna:
when the counteractive [remedy] arises, both the remedial factor and the factor to be remedied necessarily coexist.
The sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is currently arising as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*),
while the seeds of the two obstacles within the eighth *ālayavijñāna* are currently that which is to be remedied (*vipakṣa*).
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
If the ālayavijñāna did not exist,
it would be impossible for this counteractive consciousness to coexist with the seeds of the great and small afflictions.
The treatise further states:
"If one is separated from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) cannot be accomplished.
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha*) further says:
The first moment is the unimpeded path that destroys the present. Regarding the classification of the three paths:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, ordinary persons possess both the mundane path for severing fetters and the noble path, and both consist of the four paths.
First, the path of preparation;
second, the path of non-obstruction;
third, the path of liberation.
Regarding the four paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), among these four, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) is the correct abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*);
it is also said that there is the realization of liberation (*vimukti*) and the correct realization (*samyaksākṣātkriyā*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states:
"That which is called the 'pair of paths' for cessation was taught by the Blessed One.
The subsequent treatise says:
One should know that the afflictions of the three realms are extinguished by the path of liberation, which is unimpeded;
this is preceded by skillful means and assisted by subsequent progress, and is not [merely] correct abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
According to the tenets of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the severance of all fetters and latent tendencies likewise possesses the four paths.
The names are the same as before.
Within each and every path, many types of mind are described,
not merely a single category up to nine categories.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"A multitude of minds sever the various afflictions;
it is neither eight nor nine."
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are likewise four paths;
these take unimpeded application as right abandonment,
and liberation as right realization.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) is difficult to attain, liberation (*vimukti*) is difficult to attain.
It asks: [Why is this so?]
Regarding the Mahāyāna liberation through the severance of fetters and non-obstruction:
do these two paths exist within a single moment of thought,
or do they exist across two moments of thought?
The answer is:
Some Dharma masters maintain that,
in the Mahāyāna, the severing of afflictions occurs within a single thought-moment, wherein these two paths are present.
Its essential nature is truly one;
it is spoken of as two from the perspective of its meaning.
The correct severance of manifest delusions is termed "unimpeded."
To claim that this very non-obstruction prevents future afflictions from arising and is thus called "liberation" is incorrect.
If non-obstruction itself were liberation,
[then liberation would exist even while those afflictions are present].
The vajra-body of a bodhisattva is unimpeded;
it should therefore be identical to the liberation of the fruit of buddhahood.
Yet, although the vajra-mind within a single thought-moment is indeed unimpeded, it is not yet the fruit of buddhahood itself.
For what reason can it be said that a single thought-moment is unimpeded and is itself liberation?
Now, let us correctly judge this:
these two paths must necessarily be distinct thoughts.
The unimpeded nature of the preceding thought-moment is called right abandonment;
the liberation of the subsequent thought-moment is called right realization.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The first moment is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
the second moment is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The first moment destroys present afflictions, causing them to cease.
In the second moment, one obstructs future afflictions so that they do not arise.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One who practices the path of non-obstruction is called a bodhisattva."
The practice of the path of liberation is called the "various Buddhas. There are four types of abandonment through suppression and severance.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the severance of fetters within the realm of desire applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
Ordinary beings, through the six mundane practices, completely sever the two types of delusions—those of view and those of cultivation—within the desire realm.
Up to the point where the three types of emptiness are collectively severed, all such instances constitute permanent abandonment.
Regarding the distinct severance of the views and cultivations within the realm by the noble ones:
one first severs the views regarding the truths, and subsequently severs the afflictions of cultivation.
From the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these too are eternally severed.
Question: Regarding the severance of afflictions by ordinary beings and sages—
Ordinary beings do not perceive principle,
whereas the sages perceive principle.
How is it that the severance of delusions by both is equally a permanent severance?
The answer is:
Although the views of ordinary beings and noble ones regarding phenomena and principle differ, their cultivation of the path to severing fetters is the same;
both equally abandon the acquisition of delusion and cause the substance of delusion to perish so that it no longer belongs to any person.
Therefore, both ordinary beings and sages speak of "permanent abandonment.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
for an ordinary person, this is merely a conceptualization and not true wisdom.
Regarding the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), these are suppressed but not severed.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"These non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) sever their fetters, yet they arise again and are reborn in the desire realm."
Therefore, ordinary persons are not said to have severed the fetters.
Furthermore, because ordinary persons constantly possess the notion of a self,
they are unable to sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the other fetters.
Question: If ordinary beings do not sever their afflictions,
how can they be reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) at the end of their lives?
Answer: It profoundly obstructs the arising of afflictions in the form and formless realms.
According to the tenets of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, all afflictions severed by the noble ones (ārya) are severed forever.

In the Mahāyāna teachings, there may be Dharma masters who cite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, stating that certain non-Buddhists sever the fetters through the six practices and thereby become candidates for the three fruits;
they then claim that such ordinary persons have eternally severed their afflictions.
Alternatively, one may cite the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, which states:

"If various afflictions reside within sentient beings and, through the continuity of their dispassion, arise from the cause of immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*) in the two upper realms, they are termed latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)."
Alternatively, it may refer to ordinary persons who have either subdued or partially attenuated the afflictions of the "skin" level;

furthermore, it refers to the mundane state of detachment from desire, wherein the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-quiescent levels are extinguished and the latencies of the quiescent levels increase, thereby establishing the meaning of mundane *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis).
The various Dharma masters have cited the preceding text to prove that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are permanently severed within the Mahāyāna; however,
this interpretation is incorrect.
The explanations in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* accord with the Sarvāstivāda school and do not represent the correct tenets of the Mahāyāna.
As for the explanation in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding ordinary beings severing afflictions:
All these are instances of subduing the fetters (saṃyojana) which are termed "abandonment" (prahāṇa),
but they do not mean permanent abandonment.
Now, the correct determination is as follows.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, when ordinary beings sever their fetters, this is merely a suppression and severance rather than a permanent severance.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"When ordinary beings fall back from a higher realm and undergo birth in a lower realm..."
The consciousness at the initial moment of rebirth is necessarily defiled by both gross and subtle afflictions.
From what seeds do this consciousness and these afflictions arise?
In the treatise, the various masters of the Hīnayāna are thus questioned.
Since the afflictions arising in an ordinary person when descending from a higher realm to a lower realm must necessarily arise from causes,
we know that when an ordinary person is born into a higher realm from a lower stage, [the same principle applies].
Without severing the seeds of the afflictions of the view- and cultivation-stages within the *ālaya-vijñāna* of the desire realm, one is born into the higher realms;
now, returning to be born here below, one gives rise to afflictions and moistens rebirth by means of those former seeds.
Since the seeds already exist,
it should be known that they are not severed.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
The contaminated wholesome consciousness is not what is meant by the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Among the various non-Buddhists, there is the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin, but they lack the truth of cessation and the truth of the path."
Since it is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it does not sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"If one were to sever the afflictions by means of the mundane path (*saṃvṛti-mārga*)."
Although [defilements] are severed, they arise again.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The mundane path does not attain the fruit of liberation."
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, all afflictions severed by the sages— both those prior to and those upon the stages— are severed forever. Regarding the fourth point,
the similarities and differences in contemplative practice,
there are two sections therein.
First, contemplation;
second, practice.
Within the initial gate of contemplation, there are further four propositions. First, regarding the emptiness of both person and phenomena: [text continues].
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, when ordinary persons sever afflictions through conventional analytical observation, they do not realize the emptiness of both arising phenomena and dharmas.
When noble ones sever afflictions, they cultivate only the emptiness of arising beings (pudgala-śūnyatā) and do not cultivate the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā).
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"It is empty because it is internally devoid of a person.

The school of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* maintains that the noble ones, having severed their fetters, universally cultivate the contemplation of both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"To perceive merely that form and other phenomena are impermanent and subject to decay is also called 'emptiness,' but this does not refer to purity."
Later, seeing the cessation of the aggregates is the contemplation of purity.
Question: Is this the knowledge conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
For what reason does the *Xiàqīngjìng lùn* (Treatise on Lower Purity) state:
"At a later time, the practitioner gives rise to the perception of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
and that mind of provisional designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti-citta*) arises once again"?
Therefore, it is not pure.
If one realizes the cessation of the aggregates, the aggregates no longer manifest;
because they have ceased as mere designations, the perception of them as mere designations no longer follows after.
Therefore, it is called "pure.
It is like a tree that has been cut down, burned, and reduced entirely to ashes and charcoal;
once the conceptualization of the tree is completely exhausted, it no longer follows after [the object].
The *Tattvasiddhi* further states:
"According to the true meaning,
all afflictions and the like are severed at the moment their cessation is realized."
What is called the "vision of cessation" is precisely the emptiness of its own nature;
it is the cessation that is the emptiness of the dharma of nirvāṇa.

Within the Mahāyāna teachings, the two obstacles that are severed are likewise severed by practicing the contemplation of the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) to eliminate afflictions.
Prior to the Great Ground (bhūmi), one severs the afflictions within the realm [of desire] by means of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);
from the first ground upward, one severs the afflictions beyond the realm by means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
Previously, at the stage of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), one has already attained the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
now, at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
Before the stages (bhūmi), one gradually eliminates the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa);
from the attainment of the first stage upward, one gradually eliminates the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa). Second, the elucidation of the three types of wisdom:
namely, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, among the three types of wisdom, whether mundane or supramundane, one employs only cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) to sever the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
for it is through this concentrated mind that one is able to eradicate the defilements.
Distraction through hearing and reflection cannot sever the afflictions;
the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that only the wisdom of cultivation can sever the afflictions.
Because it is eternally free from names and because it is right concentration,
it is neither [the wisdom] of hearing nor of reflection.
According to the tenets of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the three types of wisdom—namely, that consisting of hearing and so forth—all sever the afflictions.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"As for the mind of conventional designation (*prajñapti-citta*):"
Some are severed through the causal condition of the wisdom of extensive learning;
some are severed through the causal condition of the wisdom of reflection.
The mind that dwells upon the true dharma within the stages of "Heat" and so forth is severed by means of the wisdom of emptiness.
In the Mahāyāna teachings as well, the two obstacles are eliminated through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
not through hearing or reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*). As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The wisdom of śamathavipaśyanā takes the synthesized dharma as its object;
moment by moment, it is able to destroy the mass of afflictions.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Stabilized, moving, knowing, subdued, and eliminated.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* further states:

"This reveals that it is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), not the wisdom of hearing or reflection (*śrutamayī- or cintāmayī-prajñā*). [It also mentions] the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and the three types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
This refers to the three types of knowledge: preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained.
Although the Sarvāstivāda school and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* discuss the knowledge that severs the fetters, they do not mention the term "preparatory knowledge."
However, the wisdom that serves as the direct antidote consists precisely of the three [types of] wisdom;
the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) is neither the fundamental body nor the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) to be abandoned within the Mahāyāna teachings:
Prior to the Great Ground (mahābhūmi), one primarily employs preparatory application (*prayoga*) as the unimpeded liberation to sever the obstacles of affliction;

because one has realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this involves only preparatory application. One has not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and thus it is not the middle or subsequent knowledges (*madhyama-paścāt-jñāna*).

From the first bhūmi upward, one employs the wisdom of the middle way as the unimpeded liberation to sever the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) along with the latencies (*vāsanā*) of both cognitive and afflictive obscurations. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"By means of non-conceptual wisdom, [the obscurations] are dispelled and extinguished."
"Sending away" refers to the present;
"extinguishing" refers to the future.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
Upon attaining non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one then resolves the fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).
As the fetters of signs do not arise, the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) are accordingly extinguished.
By this it should be known that, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, it is middle wisdom (*madhyama-jñāna*) that correctly abandons [the afflictions], rather than prior or subsequent wisdoms.
Because the prior wisdom merely acts as a guide,
while the subsequently attained wisdom can only provide subsequent assistance. He asked:
The preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) is capable of severing the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
and the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) further eliminates the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Why, then, is it not stated that the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) severs the afflictions?
The answer is:
Of the two types of wisdom mentioned previously, both reside within meditative observation; because their concentration and wisdom illuminate the principle, they are able to sever delusions.
The latter, however, emerges from observation to take conventional objects as its cognitive domain; therefore, it does not sever delusions.
Question: If it is said that the subsequently attained wisdom does not sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that subsequently attained wisdom can eliminate the obstructions of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*)?

The *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) states that the extinction of present afflictions by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*),
while the extinction of future afflictions by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The answer is:

When the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) eliminates the retribution-obscuration (*vipākāvaraṇa*), this is based on the fact that subsequent knowledge emerges from meditative equipoise; it is taught that one may freely take up or discard according to one's will, and thus it is said to eliminate the obscuration of retribution.
It does not mean that the Buddha-nature is severed by the Path of Unimpededness (*ānantarya-mārga*) while it is currently functioning.

As for the statement in the *Buddhatva-śāstra* that "subsequent wisdom can sever future afflictions," this refers to the Path of Advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) after emerging from meditative absorption; it describes the severance of future afflictions as a remote prevention (*dūra-vighna*).
It is not through unimpeded abandonment. Regarding the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)—
namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—

the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that among these four applications of mindfulness, it is through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that all fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana-kleśa) are abandoned.
It is not merely the three applications of mindfulness regarding body, sensation, and mind;
the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states that within the cultivation of wisdom, all four applications of mindfulness are fully present.
That foundation of mindfulness of dharmas is able to eliminate the afflictions because it perceives the general object;
this is not the case for the other foundations of mindfulness.
This is because they are views regarding objective spheres (*ālambana*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa* also state this in the same way.

Although the school of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* does not explicitly state that each individual application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) abandons such afflictions, [the meaning is nonetheless established].
However, that treatise states:
"The foundations of mindfulness sever the delusions of the mind regarding conventional designations.
One should know that all four foundations of mindfulness sever afflictions.
Regarding the two obstacles to be severed within the Mahāyāna Dharma,
it is solely the mindfulness of dharmas that can sever the afflictions,
not the three other foundations of mindfulness.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"By means of the wisdom of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which takes the most general dharma as its object,
the mass of afflictions is destroyed moment by moment."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
"When the practitioner contemplates and destroys the afflictions,
they take true suchness as their object through non-conceptual wisdom, unifying it into a single sphere of focus."
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way.
Such sūtras and śāstras all concern the contemplation of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna). Second, the explanation of the practitioner.
That is to say, there are sixteen [aspects]:
namely, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, non-self, and so forth.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are two types of persons: the ordinary worldling and the noble one.
When ordinary persons sever the desires of the eight stages through the six mundane practices,
because they contemplate these matters [merely as objects], they do not perceive the principle of the Truths.
Regarding what are called the "six practices":
These are the practice of austerity, the practice of coarse conduct, and the practice of obstructive conduct.
One employs any one of these three practices as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there are likewise three practices.
That is to say, one practices either tranquility (śamatha), insight (vipaśyanā), or both;
employing any one of these as the path to liberation.
This refers to the case of a noble being (ārya).
To sever the delusions of the three realms, one practices the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, which consists of sixteen aspects.
Regarding the Truth of Suffering, there are four aspects:
the aspect of suffering, the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of emptiness, and the aspect of non-self.
According to their application, one practice eliminates the delusions regarding the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya),

while four practices eliminate those regarding the truth of origination (samudaya-satya): the practice of cause (hetu-gati), the practice of origination (samudaya-gati), the practice of condition (pratyaya-gati), and the practice of existence (bhava-gati).
The four aspects of the truth of cessation:
the aspect of cessation, the aspect of excellence, the aspect of tranquility, and the aspect of detachment.
The four aspects of the truth of the path.
The practice of the path consists of the practice of the tracks, the practice of the traces,
and the practice of the vehicle. If a noble person, by means of the mundane path, severs the fetters of the path of cultivation,
they again perform the six practices as previously described.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* school maintains that the severance of the fetters of the three realms does not involve the cultivation of the two [specific] practices;
rather, what is taught in the treatise consists of only two practices,
namely, the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the practice of selflessness (*anātman*).
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"There are two kinds of practice:
the practice of emptiness and the practice of non-self."
Not perceiving a sentient being within the five aggregates is called the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Seeing that there is no self upon the aggregates is the practice of non-self (*anātman*).
If one cuts off the afflictions, these two practices alone suffice.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, there are two senses in which the afflictions within the realm of desire are said to be abandoned.
If one is a śrāvaka who abandons the afflictions of the views and the path of cultivation by means of the sixteen aspects,
this is according to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.

Śrāvakas of sharp faculties, within the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), universally sever the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) beneath the four noble truths of the three realms by means of the single practice of non-self (*anātman*).

Śrāvakas of dull faculties, throughout the sixteen moments of mind, specifically sever the eighty-eight fetters beneath the four noble truths of the three realms by means of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
The *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) states:
"Regarding the contemplation of equality, there are those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties.
If a person of sharp faculties contemplates the Four Truths in a single thought-moment, the eighty-eight afflictions are severed all at once; this is termed 'seeing the truths.'"
If a person of dull faculties contemplates in successive order,
they do not perceive the other three truths during the initial moment of contemplating suffering;
only when suffering is severed is it termed "seeing the truth."
The remainder is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
According to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*,
a śrāvaka who has severed the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) possesses the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
The severance of fetters through the cultivation of the path is likewise.
If a bodhisattva severs the afflictions within the realm of desire, they are situated in the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
If they sever the afflictions of the truths (*darśana-heya*), they do so by employing a single practice of non-self (*anātman*) to suddenly sever the afflictions of vision.
If one has severed [the afflictions] through the ten rounds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and practices the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) for the rest of one's life,
one severs them separately across the nine stages within the three realms;
it is thus within each realm.
Regarding the phrase "beyond the realm" (*dharmadhātu*):

from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, within each successive stage, one realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) and the absence of self (*anātman*), thereby severing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Fifth, the distinction between falling back and not falling back:
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are two categories: the ordinary and the noble.
Ordinary beings completely sever the two types of delusion—those of the path of seeing and those of the path of cultivation—up to and including the three emptinesses;
those of sharp faculties do not fall back once they have severed them.
If a person of dull faculties has severed [the defilements] and subsequently regresses, it is as explained in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding those who are noble ones (*ārya*), there are two [considerations]:
first, with respect to the person.
Second is that which is subject to regression.
Among the aforementioned persons,
the noble ones (ārya) pertain to all three vehicles.
Pratyekabuddhas and Buddhas possess sharp faculties and do not regress;
so too do Śrāvakas who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Among those who train, having severed the delusions regarding the truths (satyadarśana-heya),
it is taught that they do not regress, whether their faculties be sharp or dull;
for the path of seeing is swift and the path of seeing is intense.
The afflictions to be abandoned are like breaking stones; like armor entering the fray, once severed they do not retreat.
This refers to the abandonment of the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, even those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) may regress when confronted with the five desires and their afflictions.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"One first attains freedom from desire through the contemplation of impurity, but later regresses by contemplating signs of purity."
In the treatise, it is stated that there are six types of lineages among those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) encounters the five conditions for falling away and regresses even after having attained cessation. These are: the lineage of those intent on reflection (*cetana-dharman*), the lineage of those who protect [their attainment] (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*), the lineage of those who abide [in their attainment] (*sthitākampya-dharman*), the lineage of those destined for excellence (*prativedhanādharman*), and the lineage of the immovable (*akopyadharman*).
These five types of persons, having severed their original lineage, do not regress.
As for those characterized by progress,
they range from the stage of "contemplating the Dharma" up to "certain advancement."
Because the faculties have not yet reached full maturity, there is regression when encountering conditions,
as explained in detail in the treatise.
Second, the identification of what is lost.

The noble one who has regressed from the intermediate *vibhaṣā-jāti* (the state of partial realization) regresses both from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and from the noble path (*ārya-mārga*),
yet does not regress from the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor lose the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is what they say.
The Noble Path extinguishes delusions, severing them forever without remainder,
just as a vessel is shattered by a stone or as wood is consumed by fire.
It is also like the burning of a garment. Pūtimatya further stated:
"When a noble one falls away, they fall away from meditative concentration and also lose the noble path."
One regresses from the arising of afflictions and simultaneously loses the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As stated in the treatise:
"When one regresses from the noble path (*āryamārga*), one abandons liberation (*vimukti-prāpti*) and the fetter of death (*maraṇa-saṃyojana*) arises once again."
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa* both agree with the assertions of the Saugata school (*Sautrāntika*). Regarding the doctrine of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
there are two interpretations concerning whether an Arhat can fall back from the state of meditative equipoise (*madhya*).
First, in terms of persons;
second, in terms of what is lost.
Regarding "in terms of persons":
Ordinary persons undergo regression;
having regressed, they give rise to afflictions and are reborn in the desire realm.
Noble ones have severed the fetters.
Once severed, there is no regression.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Arhats and others have forever uprooted the root of craving."
From what do the fetters arise?
The *Tattvasiddhi* further states:
"The noble ones scatter, extinguish, shatter, and do not accumulate or perceive them."
Therefore, there is no falling back.
Next, in the subsequent section, both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are addressed. Question:
Regarding the tenet of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* that an ordinary person’s severance of fetters constitutes either falling away or non-falling away,
the answer is:
when an ordinary person severs the fetters, they merely suppress them and do not eliminate them permanently.
If one encounters the conditions for regression, the fetters (saṃyojana) will arise again.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Various non-Buddhists (tīrthika), having severed their fetters, give rise to them once more and are reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu)."
Therefore, ordinary persons are not said to have severed their fetters.
Second, regarding those who regress:
noble ones of dull faculties, when encountering conditions for regression, may only regress from meditative concentration but do not regress from the Noble Path.
One does not give rise to the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) nor lose the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The noble path does not regress; it is only meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) that may regress."
The power of mastery within the state of meditative concentration is not a mastery that all arhats possess.
Furthermore, by relying on this meditative concentration, such a person attains the path of an arhat.
Because one loses the outflow-free state by losing meditative concentration; it is not that there is a falling away from the outflow-free itself.
It is like a mountain of stone which the wind cannot move.
The steadfast are thus unshaken by either disparagement or praise.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, there are likewise two meanings.
The first concerns the person.
Second, the explanation of what is lost.
Regarding the statement "in terms of persons," there are ordinary and noble persons.
When ordinary beings sever their fetters, this is a suppression rather than a true severance;
regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull, they will regress even after having severed them.
As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
If one cuts off afflictions through mundane paths but they arise again, it is therefore called impermanent.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Śāriputra once practiced the bodhisattva path; due to the causal conditions of giving his eyes as an act of generosity, he regressed from the Great Vehicle and dwelt in the Lesser Vehicle."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Those of no lineage (agotra) achieve rebirth in the fortunate realms, yet repeatedly regress and repeatedly advance.
This refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are at the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) or prior to them.
Regarding the term "sage" (ārya):
"sage" encompasses the three vehicles.
Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The bhikṣu Ghoṭī lost [his realization] six times;
this refers to the fact that even among śrāvakas there is the possibility of regression.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
The six consciousnesses take external objects as their conditions through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Due to this improper mental attention, one falls away from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
As for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, they possess only sharp faculties and it is not said that they fall away.
Within the Bodhisattva Dharma, those at the stage of the Ten Faiths lack firm resolve in generating the mind [of enlightenment] and their compassionate vows are shallow;
they may regress upon encountering adverse conditions.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
When bodhisattvas are in the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), their cultivation of celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*) is not yet firm;
they largely feel weary of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), their compassion is weak and thin,
and they desire to abandon the Mahāyāna to cultivate the path of the Hīnayāna.
From the stage of the ten understandings up to the ten stages, those of the same sharp faculties will certainly never regress.
The *Bhūmivastu-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"In the presence of the lineage, there is maturation without any loss or regression."
It increases progressively.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the regression of the bodhicitta occurs due to four causes and conditions.
First, they lack the lineage because they are devoid of the bodhisattva lineage;
second, they lack the illumination of the Dharma because they are separated from virtuous spiritual friends;
third, they possess little power of wisdom because they have not yet understood the emptiness of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Fourth, the power of deficient causes: not having planted the roots of goodness that are the intrinsic nature of the various *pāramitās* in previous lives.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, there are six factors that destroy the bodhicitta."
First, stinginess regarding the Dharma;
second, giving rise to unwholesome thoughts toward sentient beings;
third, associating with evil friends.
Fourth, they do not apply themselves with diligent effort.
Fifth, they are conceited and arrogant.
Sixth, they are preoccupied with worldly affairs.
These six factors destroy the bodhicitta;
among them, the first is the fetter of stinginess.
The second is ill-will;
the third is delusion;
the fourth is indolence.
Fifth is arrogance.
Sixth, due to craving, the three poisons of affliction arise.
Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are five factors that cause one to retreat from the bodhicitta.
First, they are non-Buddhist renunciants who delight in suffering;
second, they do not cultivate the mind of great compassion;
third, they take pleasure in seeking out the faults and transgressions of Dharma masters.
Fourth, they constantly delight in remaining within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Fifth, they do not rejoice in receiving and upholding the twelvefold scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
Among these, the first is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The second is the affliction of delusion;
the third is hatred;
the fourth is craving.
Fifth is lack of faith.
As stated in that sutra, whether it be the five or the six [non-virtues], they do not merely cause one to regress from the bodhicitta and give rise to afflictions;
at the very moment they arise, one also loses the bodhisattva precepts.
These instances of falling back all occur within the stage of the ten faiths.
A question is asked:
If it is said that the spiritual lineage (gotra) does not undergo falling back, [how can this be so?]
Why is it that the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states that one abides at the limit of falling away (*parihāṇi*) during the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*)?
The answer is:
regarding what the *Saṃgrahaṇī* says about abiding at the limit of falling away—
This refers to the fact that while practicing the path within the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), one temporarily fails to progress, which is termed "retrogression.
It does not mean that one has lost one's position that it is called retrogression.
Second, the identification of what is retrogressed from.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, it is said that śrāvakas of dull faculties may regress; however,
they only regress from meditative concentration and the noble path,
but do not regress from their afflictions nor lose their unconditioned [attainment].
Question: How is it known that within that Mahāyāna Dharma,
śrāvakas of dull faculties merely regress from meditative concentration and regress from the noble path, yet do not regress from their afflictions and do not lose the unconditioned?
Answer: According to the scriptural teachings,
since it is stated that the bhikṣu Gautika experienced regression, [it follows that such regression occurs].
Therefore, they merely regress from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and regress from the noble path (*ārya-mārga*).
Furthermore, according to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
an Arhat possesses no seeds of delusion and does not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, one should know that although Mahāyāna śrāvakas may regress,
they do not regress from their afflictions nor lose their unconditioned [attainment].
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
Regarding the emptiness of sentient beings, it is like the three poisons of an arhat.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"When first entering meditative observation, all heavy habitual tendencies of the various afflictions have already been extinguished."
How could worldly consciousness arise without causes and conditions?
If that were so, these afflictions would not arise from causes, and there would be no liberation;
even the afflicted mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) would likewise have to arise without a cause.
Question: Since those above the stage of *gotra* (spiritual lineage) do not regress once they have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*),
why does the *Bhūmivastu* state that a bodhisattva of the *gotra* stage matures the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) and is not defiled by the four afflictions?
If one is defiled, pure dharmas do not manifest before them.
Since it is stated that when one is defiled, pure dharmas do not arise,
we know that the lineage (gotra) is lost, the path is definitely interrupted, afflictions arise, and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is forfeited.
As for what was previously stated regarding the absence of regression for those above the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
the answer is that from the stage of spiritual lineage upward, there is no regression in the severing of fetters, as the four aforementioned conditions do not apply.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states that if defiled white dharmas do not arise,
this does not refer to the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) on the path of cultivation within the realm [of desire].
Herein, the bodhisattva permanently eradicates the defilements arising from manifest mental states (*paryavasthāna*).
However, because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the path of cultivation and subtle afflictions manifest and obstruct the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), there is no contradiction.
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states:
"Briefly stated, there are four faults of the bodhisattva lineage."
First, regarding the cultivation of afflictions and the non-practice of merit while afflictions are frequently practiced:
since that [text] speaks of "cultivating afflictions" (*huo-xi*),
it is clear that these are not the active outbursts (*zheng-shi*).
Regarding the number of grades in the sixth chapter:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the severing of the fetters and proclivities necessarily involves nine grades.
That is to say, the path of the lowest-of-the-low grade counteracts the fetter of the highest-of-the-high grade.
Up to the point where the highest-of-the-high path severs the lowest-of-the-low fetters.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Ordinary persons sever the fetters through nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation, thereby severing the fetters of the nine grades."
The Sage’s severance of the fetters is likewise so.
It is asked:
What is the difference between ordinary persons and sages, both of whom sever the nine kinds of fetters through the ninefold path?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The afflictions severed by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are severed through a combination of the paths of seeing and cultivation;
those severed by noble persons (*ārya*) are first severed through the path of seeing the truths, and subsequently severed through the path of cultivation."
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The noble ones sever the fetters of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) by means of one path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Those [fetters] to be severed through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are severed by nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation."
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"One type is abandoned by nine types;
nine types are abandoned by one type."

The ninefold abandonment refers to the abandonment of the nine types of fetters pertaining to the truths (*satyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*). The ninefold [abandonment] is the abandonment of the fetters pertaining to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-saṃyojana*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* school, all fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through multiple moments of mind (*citta*).
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda school,
which speaks only of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and enumerates the nine grades.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
Some say that there are nine kinds of afflictions and nine kinds of wisdom;
by means of the lowest-of-the-low wisdom, one abandons the highest-of-the-high afflictions.
It is not the case that superior-superior wisdom eliminates inferior-inferior afflictions; rather,
it is by means of immeasurable minds that all afflictions are eliminated.
It is like a skilled craftsman who, holding the handle of an axe in his hand,
sees with his eyes the point where it touches;
yet he cannot distinguish how many parts of the handle have been worn away each day.
Only when one has seen exhaustion does one know that it is exhausted.
It is the same for a bhikṣu:
while practicing the Path, although he does not discriminate, "That which was exhausted today," [he nevertheless knows it].
If, regarding the various outflows (*āsrava*),
those which were exhausted yesterday, or regarding those various outflows,
only after they have been exhausted does one know that the flow has ceased.
Therefore, by means of the immeasurable minds, one exhausts all afflictions;
they are neither eight nor nine.
To say they are "not eight" is to refute the Sarvāstivāda view of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Regarding the statement that it is "not nine," this refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that there are nine grades on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, this is briefly treated through two approaches:
first, a general exposition of the nine grades.
Second, the specific explanation of the nine grades.
First, regarding the general explanation of the nine grades,
the Dharma masters of old have said:
In the Mahāyāna, when the afflictions to be abandoned are presented, reality is cited as the form and delusion is shown;
since there is no delusion to be abandoned, the nine grades are not mentioned. Some people say:
Within the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, wisdom arises in every thought-moment, and in each and every instant, one is able to destroy all afflictions; this is entirely unimpeded.
Thus, it is further explained in meaning that the path of non-obstruction constitutes liberation.
These arguments are all incorrect.
Now, I shall provide the definitive judgment based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
In the Mahāyāna, the afflictions to be abandoned are likewise of nine grades, and the noble paths that abandon them are also of nine grades;
thus, the lowest-of-the-low path counteracts the highest-of-the-high fetter.
The supreme path treats the lowest of the low fetters.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"If the inferior-grade perfuming by hearing arises, it can serve as the antidote to the superior-grade fundamental consciousness."
Furthermore, even up to the point where the superior-grade perfuming of hearing arises and is able to counteract the inferior-grade fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
"The practitioner, destroying the afflictions, takes true suchness (*tathatā*) as their object through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), making it a single, pervasive sphere."
First employ the inferior path,
next employ the middling path,
and finally employ the superior path.
For example, when one wishes to split wood in the world,
one first uses a fine wedge and subsequently uses a coarse wedge.
The *Bhūmivastu* (Dichi lun) states:
When a bodhisattva in the stage of practice through understanding practices the lower degree of patience, the aspect of activity increases;
at the middle degree of patience, it is middling;
and at the upper degree of patience, it is diminished.
When practicing superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) in this manner, one severs these marks of fault and enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) in succession.
The commentary states:
"At the time of inferior patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), one severs the 'increasing' [faults]."
The superior stage of the fetters is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
During the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*), it refers to the middle grade of afflictions (*kleśa*).
During the stage of superior patience (*adhimātrakṣānti*), "inferior" refers to the lower grade of afflictions.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Discriminative afflictions (*kleśa*) are beyond measure and calculation;
their cessation is likewise beyond measure and calculation."
This is not known by the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
it is called supreme wisdom.
This refers to the severance of the nine grades of afflictions through the Mahāyāna.
The sutras and śāstras are thus.
Regarding the second [section], the detailed explanation of the nine grades, there are briefly two approaches.
The first clarifies that which is within the realm (dhātu).
The second explains that which is outside the realm;
within the realm itself,
it accords with the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
There are two types of śrāvakas who sever the afflictions of the truths to be seen (*satyadarśana-heya*).

The first consists of those with sharp faculties who, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), use the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) alone as a single category of the path to universally sever the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the truths to be seen.

This means that among the seeds of the熏習 (vāsanā) of the three realms within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) that are to be abandoned, those pertaining to the truths of insight (*darśana-mārga*) are abandoned by the antidote in a single moment.
A question is asked:
"In the two higher realms, the afflictions of the path of insight are abandoned by these patiences (*kṣānti*)."
"Now, are there any afflictions of the truths to be seen (*satyadarśana-kleśa*) within the two upper realms that are abandoned by the patience of the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*)?
He replied:
"In the Mahāyāna Dharma, the afflictions of the truths to be seen within the two upper realms [are abandoned]."
Śrāvakas of sharp faculties employ the dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) to effect thorough abandonment.
They employ the dharma-patience regarding suffering to abandon the truths of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
One should apply this analogy accordingly to the successive stages.
Second, if one is of dull faculties, the eight patiences and eight knowledges eliminate the afflictions of the truths to be seen within the three realms.

As for the Śrāvakas, they eliminate the nine grades of fetters across the nine stages through nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation, which constitute both the path of cultivation within the realm and the elimination of those to be abandoned.
The principle is beyond doubt.
Regarding those in the stage of a bodhisattva who sever the fetters within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*),
they first sever those pertaining to the truths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and subsequently clarify the severance through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding the afflictions of those who have seen the truths (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), various sūtras and śāstras do not specify their numerical categories.
Now, I have ventured to follow the explanation in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*:
Śrāvakas of sharp faculties sever the eighty-eight afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) across the three realms by means of the contemplation of equality (*samatā-darśana*).
However, through the single thought-moment of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), it is immediately severed.

Now, by analogy, at the first moment of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vijñapti*) of a Bodhisattva, within a single kṣaṇa, one suddenly severs the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satya-darśana-heya*) within the three realms.
Faith is non-doubt.
If one has severed the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation,

then from the second thought-moment of the stage of Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) up until the stage of the many bodies during the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), these [afflictions] have merely been suppressed but not yet severed.

Because these various bodhisattvas have severed the manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) while retaining the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and because they intentionally take birth through the power of their vows, it is said that they have "subdued" them.

In their final body, within each of the nine stages of the three realms, they sever the nine grades of fetters by means of nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"When a bodhisattva in the stage of practice through understanding practices the lower degree of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), the aspect of practice increases;
when practicing the middle degree of patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), it is middling."
When practicing the higher patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), one descends [from the lower stages].
Thus, by practicing the higher patience and severing these faults, one enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) in succession.
This is what is taught in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* regarding the correct abandonment (samyak-prahāṇa) within the realm.
The Bodhisattva on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) practices in nine grades.
This is the case within the realm (dhātu).
Second, it clarifies the ten kinds of ignorance regarding the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) to be abandoned outside the realm.
According to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, this interpretation is further explained as follows:
the first ignorance, which constitutes the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), is briefly divided into three grades, namely:
skin, flesh, and heart.

At the initial moment of the first bhūmi, one uses non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of a single kṣaṇa as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) to suddenly sever the "outer" delusions;
the wisdom of the second moment serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In the third thought-moment, true wisdom continues in succession such that there is no longer any delusion to be severed.

Upon reaching the mind of the stage of abiding (*vihāra-bhūmi*), one again employs a single moment of non-conceptual wisdom as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever the delusions of the skin and flesh.
The wisdom of the second moment constitutes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In the third moment, there is no further delusion to be severed.
Upon reaching the mind of the fulfillment stage (*pūrṇa-bhūmi-citta*), one severs the delusions of the "skin" and "heart."
The above examples illustrate this.
Such are the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*). Question:
Now, this view of the principle must necessarily be continuous.
If one follows the previous explanation,
the abandonment of delusions through the three minds and three periods of the first stage would consequently constitute three distinct layers.
Is this not inconsistent with the meaning of the path of seeing? He replied:
"In the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, the duration of the path of seeing is brief."
In the Mahāyāna, the duration for realizing the principle during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is long;
therefore, the abandonment of afflictions is described in terms of three moments and three stages.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that all three moments simultaneously perceive the principle during the bodhisattva’s first stage (*bhūmi*), which constitutes the path of seeing.
From the second bhūmi onward, these are categorized as belonging to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The meaning of the abandonment of afflictions differs from what preceded;
this is fully detailed in the section on the second bhūmi.
The second [stage] consists of ignorance with its skin, flesh, and core.
In the initial mind of the second stage, non-conceptual wisdom gradually severs the nine grades of skin-delusions through the nine unimpeded [knowledges] and liberations.
After the ninth liberation, true wisdom continues in succession such that no further delusions remain to be severed.
Abiding in the nine grades of the mind, one severs the nine grades of flesh;
through the fulfillment of the nine grades of the mind, one severs the nine grades of the heart-mind.
According to the principles of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it should be understood in this way.
As it is with the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*),
so too may the principles for the stages from the third through the tenth be known.
Question: For what reason is it known that the Mahāyāna’s severing of afflictions is taught as being of nine grades, or alternatively, three grades? Answer:
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
it is taught that the afflictions are abandoned on the stages (*bhūmi*) either in three ways or in nine ways.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
One enters the first stage to eliminate the afflictions of the skin;
one abides in the first stage to eliminate the afflictions of the flesh;
and one emerges from the first stage to eliminate the afflictions of the mind.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
"When a practitioner of contemplation abandons afflictions, non-conceptual wisdom takes true suchness as its object, making them a single sphere of focus;
it first employs the inferior path."
Next, one employs the Middle Way;
finally, one employs the Supreme Way.
It is like splitting wood: first using a fine wedge, and later using a coarse wedge.
This proves the three grades;
since each of these three grades has three sub-divisions, there are nine grades in total.
In the Mahāyāna, the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) is subtle, gradual and sudden, and difficult to discern.
I have briefly indicated this much.
Regarding the seventh stage, the Stage of Cultivation and Severance (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa-bhūmi*), there is a brief exposition in ten sections.
The first is the differentiation of the two obstacles, which itself consists of two subsections.
First, clarifying the nature of the obstacles;
second, distinguishing the stages and grounds for severing the obstacles.
Regarding the first, clarifying the nature of the obstacles:
Obstructions refer to the two obstructions:
first, the afflictive obstruction, also called the obstruction of delusion;
second, the cognitive obstruction, also called the self-delusion.

Now, the four abidings (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) and the active afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) within the realm [of the three vehicles] constitute the substance of the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āvāsabhūmi*), as well as the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the three vehicles, constitute the substance of the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Second, regarding the abandonment of hindrances according to stages:
in the Sarvāstivāda school, among the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the five views and doubt are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*);
greed, hatred, delusion, and pride pervade both types of abandonment.
Attachment and other afflictions that delude one regarding the principles [of reality] are abandoned by the path of seeing;
attachment and other afflictions that obstruct phenomena are eliminated by the path of cultivation.
According to the tenets of that school, those of the two vehicles merely extinguish the obstacle of afflictions but have not yet removed the obstacle to knowledge.
Only the Buddha knows how to eliminate those cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha eliminates both defiled and non-defiled ignorance."
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The obstacles to knowledge are obstacles for an eternal duration.
What these two treatises describe is precisely the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictive obstacles.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* school’s position regarding the two obstacles to be abandoned differs from that of the Sarvāstivāda.

According to the tenets of that treatise, the delusions of provisional designation are abandoned during the stages of wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
In the stage of cultivating wisdom, one abandons the delusions regarding real dharmas.
Within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), at the moment of seeing cessation (*nirodha*), one abandons the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that obscure the principle.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one abandons the four underlying tendencies—namely, greed and so forth—that obscure the phenomena of each respective stage.
According to that school’s own system, among human beings,
one person of the "faith-practitioner" (śraddhānusārin) among the twenty-seven noble ones (ārya-pudgala) abandons the delusions of nominal designation (prajñapti-saṃvṛti),
while one person of the "dharma-practitioner" (dharmānusārin) abandons the delusions of substantial dharmas (dravyadharma).
The practitioner of signlessness abandons the delusions of the truths to be realized (*satyadarśana-heya*).
Of the former two types of persons, the first is one who has set out toward *srotāpanna*,
while the third is one who is close to becoming a *srotāpanna*.
Previously, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the seven preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) prior to the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*) did not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Now, according to this *Tattvasiddhi*, the five preparatory paths prior to the realization of the truths do sever the afflictions.
This refers to the two kinds of afflictions previously mentioned: those consisting of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and those consisting of substantial dharmas (*dravya*).

If one practices the path, there are twenty-four types of persons, ranging from those who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) at the stage of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to the *arhat*.
One abandons the four latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) belonging to those nine stages.
According to the tenets of that treatise, since hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms, it is said that there are four latent tendencies. Question:
Since provisional names (*prajñapti*) and real dharmas (*dravya-dharma*) have already been explained as two distinct afflictions apart from the ten proclivities (*daśānuśaya*),
it remains unknown what the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these afflictions is.
The answer is as follows:
These two delusions are common to all three realms;
the former is the delusion of a personal self (pudgala-ātman), and the latter is the delusion of a phenomenal self (dharma-ātman).
Because they are light, the ten afflictions (āsrava) are severed prior to the realization of the truths (satyadarśana);
because they are distinct and heavy, the afflictions of the path of vision (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) are severed separately.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, at the time one attains the two types of cessation (nirodha), that mind of emptiness is extinguished.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"If one takes nirvāṇa as an object of cognition, this is called the 'emptiness of mind.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* further states:
The empty mind ceases in two places:
first, it ceases when entering a mindless meditative absorption;
second, it ceases when entering nirvana without remainder, whereby the continuity [of existence] is severed.
In the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*), it ceases because its object is cessation.
At the time of severing the continuity, it ceases because its cause is exhausted.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, there is one type of afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), correctly severs the superficial delusions (*tvag-moha*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
as well as the superficial delusions of the path of cultivation in the four dhyānas and the three formless absorptions (*trayo ’rūpyasamāpattayaḥ*).

During the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-nirvedhabhāgīya*), he universally severs the substantial delusions (*māṃsa-moha*) regarding the truths (*satya*) of the three realms (*traidhātuka*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), the first five stages serve only to sever the "outer" delusions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Some monks of the Jin and Han periods have asserted that the stage of subduing [delusions] prior to the stages (*sambhāra-bhūmi*) cannot sever these delusions.
The Sūtras state:
"There are those who appear in the world who possess the nature of afflictions.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing) state:
Because the bodhi of subduing the mind is said to be the patience of subduing (伏忍),
it is taught that prior to the stages (地前) there is only subduing and no severance;
it is only upon reaching the first stage (初地) that one severs the afflictions of the view-corresponding active outflows (見修正使煩惱) within the realm of desire.
The first stage (bhūmi) abandons the afflictions of views;
from the second stage onward, one abandons those of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Alternatively, among the various Dharma masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, some say:
The claim that one abandons the delusions of the truths (satyadarśana-heya) during the stage of the ten understandings (daśa-avabodha),
and only upon ascending to the first ground (bhūmi) does one abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the realms, is incorrect.

For if the Tripiṭaka masters were to say that one has already abandoned the afflictions of the path of cultivation in the desire realm during the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā), [it would contradict their own teachings].

Furthermore, it is stated that those who sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the four dhyānas and three formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) are ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) bodhisattvas during the stage of the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā), who possess only outflowing (sāsrava) consciousnesses. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
it is not admitted that outflowing wholesome consciousnesses undergo the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) consist of pure dharmas intermingled with discordant dharmas.
How then can the Tripiṭaka masters say that ordinary beings in those ten stages of faith sever their afflictions?
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, the severing of delusions involves first seeing [the truth] and subsequently practicing.
Why, then, is this [stage] one where practice comes first and seeing follows?
Moreover, from the stage of the Ten Understandings upward, the Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages apply their minds to the path of severing and practicing.
Leaving behind the seeds of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the three realms,
he undergoes births in the three realms to spontaneously benefit sentient beings;
now, having attained the stage of the Ten Faiths, he has already severed the "outer skin" delusions.
Furthermore, what afflictions do the bodhisattvas retain that cause them to undergo birth within the three realms?
Is this not also erroneous?
The Tripiṭaka Master further says:

Regarding the first five of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), it is proclaimed that they sever only the "outer" delusions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Although this proclamation exists,
upon privately examining the treatises, I have not seen any textual passage that accepts this view.
It is unknown upon what sūtras or śāstras the Tripiṭaka Master based this interpretation.

As for the statement by the monks of the Jin and Han periods that those prior to the stages (bhūmi) have suppressed their delusions but have not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state: [text follows]?

Before the stages (bhūmi), one gradually abandons the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa); from the first stage (prathamabhūmi) upward, one gradually eliminates the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas.
The first is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
which refers to those from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and below.
The second is the noble one (*ārya*),
referring to those from the stage of ten-fold understanding (*daśa-vidyā*) upward.
Here, it is clarified that the basis of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is transformed into the basis of a noble one.
Since the treatise already states that one gradually abandons the obstacles of afflictions prior to the stages (*bhūmi*),
